message:
fix(update): the host now watches the working copy, not only the bootstrap's exit code

Reading the bootstrap's exit correctly was half of it. After the handover
there was nothing left being watched except a signal that might never
come, so a working copy that died mid-download cost the host the entire
ten-minute timeout -- and the reason it eventually gave was "did not reach
a verified download in time", which is true of a crash and of a slow link
alike.

The working copy holds a mutex named from the same stem for as long as it
lives, and the host waits on it alongside the ready event. A mutex rather
than an event because the property wanted is "this process still exists",
and that is what a mutex gives for nothing: when the holder dies the wait
is released -- abandoned, but released. Nothing has to remember to signal
on the way out, which is the point, since the death worth catching is the
one that runs no cleanup. The bootstrap must not hold it; its exit means
nothing, and a name held by that process would report a death every time.

Measured: a worker that dies is noticed in 328ms against a 20s deadline,
with its own reason. With the tracking removed it takes the full 20000ms
and the reason collapses into the timeout.

Two mistakes of mine, both caught by measurement rather than by reading.
Slicing the wait meant asking the decision function on every slice, so
"nothing has happened yet" became a final answer and the wait ended after
the first 100ms -- the loop was reporting its own patience as a failure.
And the timing assertion measured the whole attempt, which includes this
test polling the witness afterwards: it was measuring the test's patience
rather than the product's.
